claim: A 2 hr period of food deprivation robustly enhances subsequent food intake in larval zebrafish.
source: A 2 hr period of food deprivation robustly enhances subsequent food intake (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased gut fluorescence and hunting behavior in food-deprived fish compared to fed fish (Figure 1a).

claim: Food-deprived animals display a strong upregulation of hunting and prey intake relative to continuously fed fish up to 15 min after the presentation of prey.
source: Up to 15 min after the presentation of prey, food-deprived animals display a strong upregulation of hunting and prey intake relative to fish that have continuous access to food (referred to as fed fish; Figure 1a), on the basis of fluorescent food ingestion (left panel, Figure 1a) and hunting bouts (right panel, Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of gut fluorescence and hunting bout probability shown in Figure 1a.

claim: As fish consume food, their rate of food intake declines to that of continuously fed fish.
source: Finally, as the fish consume food, their rate of food intake declines to that of continuously fed fish (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing convergence of hunting bout probability over time (Figure 1a).

claim: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) shows enhanced activity during voracious feeding that follows food deprivation.
source: Relative activation from feeding after food deprivation yields activated regions including the telencephalon (Tel), Arborization field 7 (AF7), cerebellum (CB), hindbrain (HB), Vagal ganglion (VG) and lateral lobe of the intermediate hypothalamus (LH).
evidence: Supported by MAP-mapping difference analysis showing increased pERK activity in LH (Figure 1b-d).

claim: The caudal hypothalamus (cH) shows reduced activity during voracious feeding that follows food deprivation.
source: Reduced activity was observed in the caudal hypothalamus (cH) and some areas of the telencephalon.
evidence: Supported by MAP-mapping difference analysis showing decreased pERK activity in cH (Figure 1b-d).

claim: Food-deprived fish consistently displayed higher LH and lower cH pERK fluorescence after the onset of feeding.
source: Food-deprived fish consistently displayed higher LH and lower cH pERK fluorescence after the onset of feeding (p = 0.0019 for both cH and LH, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Supported by ROI-specific pixel intensity analysis across nine independent experiments (Figure 1c).

claim: The zebrafish LH does not harbor melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH)-positive or orexin (hypocretin)-positive neurons.
source: However, the zebrafish LH, unlike its mammalian counterpart, does not harbor melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH)-positive, orexin (hypocretin)-positive neurons, or other major feeding-related peptides (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and transgenic labeling showing absence of MCH and HCRT in zebrafish LH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The zebrafish LH contains glutamatergic and GABAergic cell types.
source: The zebrafish LH region does however contain glutamatergic and GABAergic cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by transgenic labeling showing VGlut2a and GAD1b expression in LH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Mean fluorescence in the cH was significantly increased in food-deprived fish.
source: Using these respective metrics, we observed that mean fluorescence in the cH was significantly increased in food-deprived fish, while the number of active neurons in the medial and lateral lobes of the LH (mLH and lLH, respectively) was relatively low (Figure 1f–h).
evidence: Supported by quantification of anti-pERK fluorescence intensity in isolated brains (Figure 1f-h).

claim: Enhanced pERK activity during food deprivation in the cH was most prevalent in serotonergic neurons.
source: Within the cH, enhanced pERK activity during food deprivation was most prevalent in serotonergic neurons, but also present in a smaller proportion of dopaminergic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by co-staining with anti-5-HT and anti-pERK antibodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).

claim: During voracious feeding following food deprivation, the pERK-reported activity of cH neurons fell dramatically to a level significantly below that observed in continuously fed fish.
source: During the period of voracious feeding that followed food deprivation, the pERK-reported activity of cH neurons fell dramatically to a level significantly below that observed in continuously fed fish (Figure 1f–h).
evidence: Supported by quantification of anti-pERK fluorescence showing reduced cH activity during feeding (Figure 1f-h).

claim: LH neuronal activity increased during voracious feeding and lasted throughout the period of voracious feeding.
source: This characteristically low cH activity level coincided with a large increase in LH activity, measured by either mean anti-pERK fluorescence or by measurement of the number of individually active neurons, that lasted throughout the period of voracious feeding.
evidence: Supported by quantification of LH active cell count and fluorescence intensity (Figure 1f-h).

claim: After 30 min of feeding, neural activity in both the cH and LH had mostly converged to the baseline level observed for continuously fed fish.
source: After 30 min of feeding, neural activity in both the cH and LH had mostly converged to the baseline level observed for continuously fed fish, consistent with the time course of hunting behavior reduction (Figure 1a, right panel).
evidence: Supported by time course data showing convergence of activity levels (Figure 1a, Figure 1i).

claim: cH activity increased following food removal, with an especially large anti-pERK average fluorescence intensity increase after 2 hrs of food deprivation.
source: Following food removal, cH activity increased, with an especially large anti-pERK average fluorescence intensity increase after 2 hrs of food deprivation (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: Supported by quantification of normalized pERK intensity across different food deprivation durations (Figure 2a-b).

claim: Food removal quickly reduced the frequency of active mLH and lLH neurons.
source: In contrast to the cH, food removal quickly reduced the frequency of active mLH and lLH neurons (Figure 2a,c).
evidence: Supported by active cell count quantification showing reduced LH activity during food deprivation (Figure 2a,c).

claim: The addition of prey rapidly reversed the food deprivation-induced patterns of cH and LH neural activity, with an amplitude of change that was correlated with the length of food deprivation.
source: Notably, the addition of prey (paramecia) rapidly reversed the food deprivation- induced patterns of cH and LH neural activity, with an amplitude of change that was correlated with the length of food deprivation (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–e).
evidence: Supported by quantification showing greater changes in activity after longer food deprivation periods (Figure 2a-c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Fish that had been food-deprived for longer periods (2 hr or 4 hr) displayed a greater increase in the number of active LH neurons compared to feeding animals that had been food-deprived for only 30 min.
source: Fish that had been food-deprived for longer periods (2 hr or 4 hr) displayed a greater increase in the number of active LH neurons compared to feeding animals that had been food-deprived for only 30 min (Figure 2a–c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–e).
evidence: Supported by active cell count data showing correlation between deprivation duration and LH activation (Figure 2a-c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The presence of highly active neurons in the LH was correlated with higher food consumption.
source: In general, the presence of highly active neurons in the LH was correlated with higher food consumption (as measured by gut fluorescence, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between LH activity and gut fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Tg(116A:Gal4) drives expression mainly in serotonergic neurons of the cH (88.9 ± 0.8% 5-HT positive) and paraventricular organ (PVO).
source: The 116A:Gal4 transgene drives expression mainly in serotonergic neurons of the cH (88.9 ± 0.8% 5-HT positive) and paraventricular organ (PVO; Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by quantification of overlap between Tg(116A:Gal4) expression and anti-5-HT staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Tg(76A:Gal4) drives expression in a large proportion of LH cells.
source: whereas 76A:Gal4 drives expression in a large proportion of LH cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Muto et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by imaging showing Tg(76A:Gal4) expression pattern and citation to previous characterization (Muto et al., 2017).

claim: Paramecia presentation increases activity in the LH and reduces activity in the cH within seconds.
source: Paramecia presentation increases activity in the LH and reduces activity in the cH, revealing opposing activity on short timescales.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging traces showing rapid opposing changes in cH and LH activity upon paramecia presentation (Figure 3b).

claim: An increase in LH activity and corresponding reduction in cH activity is observable within seconds of paramecia presentation.
source: An increase in LH activity and corresponding reduction in cH activity is observable within seconds of paramecia presentation, except for fish D in which maximal responses only occur after a few minutes (beyond the displayed time window).
evidence: Supported by high temporal resolution calcium imaging data (Figure 3b).

claim: Average Δf/f triggered on lLH calcium spikes shows a mean corresponding reduction in cH activity.
source: Average Δf/f triggered on lLH calcium spikes (left and right lobes averaged) shows a mean corresponding reduction in cH activity (n = 159 lLH spikes extracted from mean Δf/f traces from 14 fish across the entire duration of the experiment).
evidence: Supported by spike-triggered average analysis showing anti-correlated activity (Figure 3c).

claim: Water alone was sufficient to significantly reduce cH integrated fluorescence and spike frequency but not spike amplitude.
source: Water alone was sufficient to significantly reduce cH integrated fluorescence (p = 6.1×10−5) and spike frequency (p = 0.0127) but not spike amplitude (p = 0.9324).
evidence: Supported by quantification of calcium imaging metrics comparing baseline to water delivery (Figure 3e).

claim: Water alone was sufficient to increase lLH integrated fluorescence and spike frequency but not spike amplitude.
source: Water alone was similarly sufficient to increase lLH integrated fluorescence (p = 0.029) and spike frequency (p = 0.0098) but not spike amplitude (p = 0.13).
evidence: Supported by quantification of calcium imaging metrics comparing baseline to water delivery (Figure 3e).

claim: Paramecia delivery significantly increased mLH and lLH integrated fluorescence and spike frequency relative to water delivery.
source: Paramecia delivery significantly increased mLH and lLH integrated fluorescence (mLH, p = 1.2×10−4; lLH, p = 0.045) and spike frequency (mLH, p = 6.1×10−5; lLH, 6.1 × 10−4), while only significantly increasing mLH spike amplitude (mLH, p = 0.045; lLH, p = 0.43), relative to water delivery.
evidence: Supported by quantification of calcium imaging metrics comparing water to paramecia delivery (Figure 3e).

claim: Paramecia delivery significantly reduced cH integrated fluorescence relative to water delivery alone.
source: In contrast, paramecia delivery significantly reduced cH integrated fluorescence relative to water delivery alone (p = 3.1×10−4), but not spike frequency (p = 0.52) nor spike amplitude (p = 0.85).
evidence: Supported by quantification of calcium imaging metrics comparing water to paramecia delivery (Figure 3e).

claim: The cH and LH voxels were mostly anti-correlated, whereas voxels within each cluster displayed correlated activity.
source: The cH and LH voxels were mostly anti-correlated, whereas voxels within each cluster displayed correlated activity.
evidence: Supported by cross-correlogram analysis of hypothalamic voxels (Figure 3f).

claim: There is a four-fold probability relative to chance of the most anti-correlated voxels to cH voxels being part of the lLH.
source: For example, if we consider all the voxels within the cH, there is a four-fold probability relative to chance of their most anti-correlated voxels (Rank = 1) being part of the lLH.
evidence: Supported by quantification of anti-correlation probability across 14 fish (Figure 3g).

claim: Artemia exposure caused significant increases in both mLH and lLH activity, whereas little change was detected in cH neurons.
source: We found that artemia exposure caused significant increases in both mLH and lLH activity, whereas little change was detected in cH neurons (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: Supported by pERK-based activity mapping comparing artemia to control conditions (Figure 4a-c).

claim: Exposure to paramecia triggered an even larger response in both LH lobes and led to a significant reduction in cH activity compared to artemia.
source: Exposure to paramecia on the other hand triggered an even larger response in both LH lobes and led, as expected, to a significant reduction in cH activity.
evidence: Supported by pERK-based activity mapping comparing paramecia to artemia conditions (Figure 4a-c).

claim: The mLH displayed a much larger response to artemia than the lLH when the frequency of active neurons was compared.
source: However, when the frequency of active neurons was compared, the mLH displayed a much larger response (θA/θP = 32%) to artemia than the lLH (θA/θP = 15%) (Figure 4c, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by active cell count quantification comparing artemia and paramecia responses (Figure 4c).

claim: The mLH appears to be the most highly tuned to prey detection in the absence of prey ingestion.
source: Taken together with our calcium imaging results (Figure 3), these observations indicate that while all three hypothalamic regions (cH, mLH and lLH) are modulated by prey sensory cues, they respond more strongly to prey ingestion. Among these regions, the mLH appears to be the most highly tuned to prey detection in the absence of prey ingestion (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by comparison of artemia and paramecia responses across hypothalamic regions (Figure 4a-d).

claim: Optogenetic excitation of cH neurons is sufficient to inhibit LH neural activity.
source: As an initial test of this hypothesis, we determined whether optogenetic excitation of cH neurons would be sufficient to inhibit LH neural activity.
evidence: This is the stated experimental goal that is subsequently tested.

claim: Tg(y333:Gal4) drives ReaChR expression in a large fraction of cH serotonergic neurons (57.4 ± 2.1%).
source: The Tg(y333:Gal4) line drives ReaChR expression in a large fraction of cH serotonergic neurons (57.4 ± 2.1%; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), as well as a smaller fraction of dopaminergic cells (23.9 ± 2.2%; up to 30% overlap observed, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantification of overlap between Tg(y333:Gal4) expression and cell type markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1-2).

claim: ReaChR activation in the cH was sufficient to induce cH neural activity.
source: We showed that ReaChR activation in the cH was sufficient to induce cH neural activity (Figure 5a,c).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing increased cH activity following laser illumination (Figure 5a,c).

claim: ReaChR activation significantly reduced spontaneous lLH calcium spike activity within a 90 s period that followed laser illumination.
source: In contrast, ReaChR activation significantly reduced spontaneous lLH calcium spike activity within a 90 s period that followed laser illumination (Figure 5b,d), whereas no significant decrease was observed in mLH activity (Figure 5b,d).
evidence: Supported by quantification of calcium activity metrics before and after optogenetic stimulation (Figure 5b,d).

claim: Illumination of a control preoptic area region did not affect lLH activity.
source: Illumination of a control preoptic area region, where Tg(y333:Gal4)-driven ReaChR is not expressed, did not affect lLH activity, though we did observe a small increase in mLH activity (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by quantification of calcium activity in control region stimulation experiments (Figure 5e).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of cH neural activity is sufficient to inhibit lLH neural activity.
source: In sum, optogenetic stimulation of cH neural activity is sufficient to inhibit lLH neural activity, consistent with the notion that cH and LH regions interact to modulate the animal's motivational state in response to food deprivation and feeding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic experiments described in Figure 5.

claim: Animals expressing ReaChR in cH neurons that were illuminated during a short period of food deprivation subsequently consumed significantly more paramecia than control fish.
source: As expected, animals that had been illuminated during a short period of food deprivation subsequently consumed significantly more paramecia than control fish, which were similarly food-deprived and illuminated, but lacked the ReaChR transgene (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by quantification of gut fluorescence showing increased food intake after cH stimulation in 30 min food-deprived fish (Figure 6a).

claim: Fish that had been illuminated at the end of a two-hour food deprivation period displayed a high level of prey ingestion irrespective of whether the ReaChR channel was present.
source: In contrast, fish that had been illuminated at the end of a two-hour food deprivation period displayed a high level of prey ingestion irrespective of whether the ReaChR channel was present.
evidence: Supported by quantification showing no significant difference between ReaChR+ and ReaChR- fish after 2 hr food deprivation (Figure 6a).

claim: Optogenetic activation of cH neurons during feeding in 2 hr food-deprived fish reduces food intake.
source: Optogenetic activation of Tg(y333:Gal4; UAS:ReaChR-RFP) fish during feeding in 2 hr food-deprived fish reduces food intake: n = 53/44 (ReaChR-/ReaChR+), p = 0.042.
evidence: Supported by quantification of gut fluorescence showing reduced food intake after cH stimulation during feeding (Figure 6b).

claim: Nitroreductase-mediated ablation of the cH significantly enhances food intake in both fed and food-deprived fish.
source: Nitroreductase-mediated ablation of the cH in Tg(116A:Gal4;UAS:nfsb-mCherry)-positive or negative fish treated with metronidazole (MTZ) from 5 to 7 dpf significantly enhances food intake in 8 dpf fish. p = 0.0042/0.041/1.4 × 10−5 (fed control vs fed ablated, 2 hr dep. control vs 2 hr dep. ablated, fed vs 2 hr dep.), n = 29 (fed control)/28 (fed ablated)/22 (dep. control)/29 (dep. ablated), two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
evidence: Supported by quantification of gut fluorescence in ablated versus control fish (Figure 6c).

claim: Animals with ablated cH serotonergic neurons displayed greater food ingestion than control animals irrespective of whether the animals had been food-deprived or continuously fed.
source: Fish with ablated cH serotonergic neurons displayed greater food ingestion than control animals irrespective of whether the animals had been food-deprived or continuously fed (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by quantification of gut fluorescence showing increased food intake in both fed and food-deprived ablated fish (Figure 6c).

claim: Stimulation of ventromedial hypothalamic loci in rodents and cats reduced feeding.
source: For example, while stimulation of ventromedial hypothalamic loci in rodents and cats reduced feeding, activation of more lateral hypothalamic loci increased both hunting behavior and food intake (Anand and Brobeck, 1951; Brobeck et al., 1956; Delgado and Anand, 1952; Krasne, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical studies on hypothalamic stimulation effects.

claim: Activation of lateral hypothalamic loci in rodents and cats increased both hunting behavior and food intake.
source: For example, while stimulation of ventromedial hypothalamic loci in rodents and cats reduced feeding, activation of more lateral hypothalamic loci increased both hunting behavior and food intake (Anand and Brobeck, 1951; Brobeck et al., 1956; Delgado and Anand, 1952; Krasne, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical studies on hypothalamic stimulation effects.

claim: Lateral hypothalamic lesions were found to reduce feeding to the point of starvation.
source: Conversely, lateral hypothalamic lesions were found to reduce feeding to the point of starvation, whereas medial hypothalamic lesions resulted in overeating (Anand and Brobeck, 1951; Hoebel, 1965; Teitelbaum and Epstein, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical lesion studies.

claim: Medial hypothalamic lesions resulted in overeating.
source: Conversely, lateral hypothalamic lesions were found to reduce feeding to the point of starvation, whereas medial hypothalamic lesions resulted in overeating (Anand and Brobeck, 1951; Hoebel, 1965; Teitelbaum and Epstein, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical lesion studies.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamus were observed to be activated during feeding and essential for enhanced food intake during hunger.
source: For example, GABAergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamus were observed to be activated during feeding and essential for enhanced food intake during hunger (Jennings et al., 2015; Stuber and Wise, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent optogenetic and electrophysiological studies.

claim: Larval zebrafish hunt prey such as paramecia through a sequence of motor actions that has been considered a hardwired reflex response to external prey stimuli.
source: Larval zebrafish hunt prey such as paramecia through a sequence of motor actions that has been considered a hardwired reflex response to external prey stimuli (Bianco et al., 2011; Semmelhack et al., 2015; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies on zebrafish hunting.

claim: Evidence has emerged that zebrafish hunting behavior is flexibly modulated by satiation state.
source: Only recently has evidence emerged that this behavior is flexibly modulated by satiation state (Filosa et al., 2016; Jordi et al., 2015; Jordi et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies showing state-dependent modulation of hunting.

claim: Larvae at 7 days post-fertilization (dpf) display enhanced hunting and enhanced food intake after a period of food deprivation.
source: and that larvae at 7 days post-fertilization (dpf) display enhanced hunting and enhanced food intake after a period of food deprivation.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation that motivates the current study.

claim: The lateral and medial hypothalamic regions came to be regarded as 'hunger' and 'satiety' centers, respectively.
source: Thus, the lateral and medial hypothalamic regions came to be regarded as 'hunger' and 'satiety' centers, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of historical scientific consensus based on the cited lesion and stimulation studies.

claim: The hypothalamus is a highly conserved central convergence point for the neural and biochemical pathways that underlie appetite regulation.
source: The hypothalamus is a highly conserved central convergence point for the neural and biochemical pathways that underlie this regulatory mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge about hypothalamic function.

claim: The regulated intake of food based on caloric needs is a fundamental homeostatically controlled process that is essential for health and survival.
source: The regulated intake of food based on caloric needs is a fundamental homeostatically controlled process that is essential for health and survival.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: The cH and LH form mutually antagonistic functional units that dominate different phases of hunger and drive appropriate behavioral responses during each phase.
source: Finally, we test the hypothesis that the cH and LH form mutually antagonistic functional units that dominate different phases of hunger and drive appropriate behavioral responses during each phase (Figure 6).
evidence: This is the central hypothesis being tested through optogenetic and ablation experiments.

claim: The degree of cH inhibition during voracious feeding is proportional to the degree of cH activation prior to feeding.
source: Based on observed cH dynamics, we propose that the degree of cH inhibition during voracious feeding is proportional to the degree of cH activation prior to feeding.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed correlation between food deprivation duration and subsequent activity changes.

claim: The release of serotonin/other neuromodulators over the course of food deprivation may be capable of sensitizing the LH even in the absence of food cues.
source: This could be mediated by the release of serotonin/other neuromodulators over the course of food deprivation, which may be capable of sensitizing the LH even in the absence of food cues.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain how hunger state is retained.

claim: During food deprivation, the cH may play complementary roles such as the sensitization of the LH and/or other feeding-related circuits, or drive alternative behavioral programs, like foraging or energy-conserving measures.
source: Thus, during food deprivation, the cH may play complementary roles such as the sensitization of the LH and/or other feeding-related circuits (as discussed above), or drive alternative behavioral programs, like foraging or energy-conserving measures (see Appendix 1 - Conceptual Circuit Model for a more in-depth discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential cH functions during food deprivation.

claim: cH neurons might generally encode a negative valence state, of which being hungry in the absence of food is an example.
source: Given that cH neurons are also activated by aversive stimuli (Randlett et al., 2015; Wee et al., 2019), they might generally encode a negative valence state, of which being hungry in the absence of food is an example.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cH neurons respond to both food deprivation and aversive stimuli, supported by citations.

claim: The silence of cH neurons in a hungry fish where food is present may imply a positive valence state.
source: The silence of these neurons in a hungry fish where food is present may then imply a positive valence state, a notion that is in ready agreement with human subjective experience.
evidence: This is an inference about the valence encoding of cH neurons based on their activity patterns.

claim: The cH functions have been proposed to be adopted by the serotonergic raphe nucleus in mammals.
source: Although the cH does not have an exact mammalian homolog, its functions have been proposed to be adopted by other modulatory populations, such as the serotonergic raphe nucleus in mammals (Gaspar and Lillesaar, 2012; Lillesaar, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations proposing evolutionary relationships between zebrafish cH and mammalian raphe.

claim: Serotonin is released during food deprivation and can enhance food-seeking behavior.
source: While shown to be a potent appetite suppressant, serotonin is also released during food deprivation, and can enhance food-seeking behavior (Elipot et al., 2013; Kantak et al., 1978; Pollock and Rowland, 1981; Voigt and Fink, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing dual roles of serotonin in appetite regulation.

claim: Inhibition of the LH impairs prey capture in zebrafish.
source: This notion is supported by Muto et al. (2017) who recently demonstrated that inhibition of the LH impairs prey capture, a behavior that is clearly related to voracious feeding.
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study showing LH function in prey capture.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the lateral recess nuclei in adult cichlids and bluegills can elicit feeding behavior.
source: Furthermore, electrical stimulation of the homologous region (lateral recess nuclei) in adult cichlids and bluegills (Demski, 1973; Demski and Knigge, 1971) can elicit feeding behavior, which is consistent with our hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to electrical stimulation studies in other fish species.

claim: Electrical or optogenetic stimulation of LH neurons in mammals triggers voracious feeding.
source: In mammals, electrical or optogenetic stimulation of LH neurons triggers voracious feeding, again consistent with our findings that the LH is highly activated during the voracious feeding phase in hungry fish (Delgado and Anand, 1952).
evidence: Supported by citation to mammalian stimulation studies.

claim: GABAergic neurons that do not co-express MCH or Orexin in the mammalian LH have been shown to be responsive to food cues and are sufficient to stimulate food intake.
source: In particular, GABAergic neurons that do not co-express MCH or Orexin have been shown to be responsive to food cues and are sufficient to stimulate food intake in mammals (Jennings et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a mammalian study characterizing LH GABAergic neurons.

claim: Many of the cH neurons are cerebrospinal fluid-contacting and thus have access to circulatory nutrient and hormone information.
source: Notably, many of the cH neurons are cerebrospinal fluid-contacting and thus have access to circulatory nutrient and hormone information (Lillesaar, 2011; Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations describing anatomical features of cH neurons.

claim: The cH and PVO express dopaminergic and a much smaller fraction of histaminergic neurons, which appear to be densely interconnected.
source: The cH and PVO also express dopaminergic (intermingled with 5-HT) and a much smaller fraction of histaminergic neurons, which appear to be densely interconnected (Chen et al., 2016; Kaslin and Panula, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations describing cell type composition of cH and PVO.

claim: Ingestive behavior comprises a series of sequential phases: initiation, procurement, and consummatory phases.
source: Ingestive behavior has been proposed to comprise a series of sequential phases: 1) the initiation phase, triggered by energy deficit, in which the animal begins to forage; 2) the procurement phase, triggered by the presence of food sensory cues, in which the animal seeks and pursues food; and 3) the consummatory phase, which usually involves more stereotyped motor programs (Berthoud, 2002; Watts, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical frameworks for understanding feeding behavior.

claim: In mammals, LH neurons are responsive to both external food sensory cues and consummatory cues.
source: In mammals, LH neurons are responsive to both external food sensory cues and consummatory cues (Jennings et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a mammalian study characterizing LH neuron responses.

claim: The LH lobes in zebrafish respond to both sensory and consummatory food cues.
source: Here, we show that the LH lobes in zebrafish also respond to both types of food cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the artemia vs paramecia experiments.

claim: The greatest enhancement of LH activity was observed almost immediately (milliseconds to seconds) after paramecia consumption.
source: While it is unclear which consummatory cues modulate LH and cH activity, based on live imaging results from Muto et al. (2017), the greatest enhancement of LH activity was observed almost immediately (milliseconds to seconds) after paramecia consumption.
evidence: Supported by citation to live imaging results from another study.

claim: The consummatory cue modulating LH activity is likely a fast pregastric signal (taste/tactile/swallowing), rather than postgastric absorption or hormone secretion.
source: Thus, the cue is likely a fast pregastric signal (taste/tactile/swallowing), rather than postgastric absorption or hormone secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid timescale of LH activation after consumption.

claim: The lLH is more sensitive to consummatory cues than sensory food cues, similar to the cH.
source: Especially in terms of cellular pERK activity, the lLH is more weakly activated by food sensory cues compared to the mLH, suggesting that the lLH, similar to the cH, may be more sensitive to consummatory cues than sensory food cues alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential responses of lLH and mLH to artemia vs paramecia.

claim: The activation state of the cH is a crucial regulator of satiation state-dependent food intake.
source: In particular, we show that the activation state of the cH is a crucial regulator of satiation state-dependent food intake.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic and ablation experiments.

claim: Artificial cH activation in satiated fish prior to feeding is sufficient to drive subsequent voracious feeding.
source: Artificial cH activation in satiated fish prior to feeding is sufficient to drive subsequent voracious feeding.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments showing increased food intake (Figure 6a).

claim: The acute effect of cH activation during feeding is suppression of food intake.
source: We furthermore show that the acute effect of cH activation during feeding is suppression of food intake, whereas cH ablation enhances food intake, which is again consistent with mammalian studies of medial hypothalamic areas.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation and ablation experiments (Figure 6b-c).

claim: Once food is presented to a hungry fish, high activity in the cH may suppress LH activity, and hence elevate the initial threshold for food intake.
source: However, the critical difference here is the presence or absence of food. Once food is presented to a hungry fish, high activity in the cH may simply suppress LH activity, and hence elevate the initial threshold for food intake.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to reconcile the seemingly paradoxical roles of cH during hunger.

claim: The medial-lateral logic of hypothalamic function that is well established in mammalian systems may be conserved even in non-mammalian vertebrates.
source: We argue that the medial-lateral logic of hypothalamic function that is well established in mammalian systems may be conserved even in non-mammalian vertebrates, though their activity patterns might possibly be more complex than originally believed.
evidence: This is a concluding statement summarizing the evolutionary conservation of hypothalamic organization.

claim: Investigating large-scale network dynamics can reveal an additional layer of insight into the principles underlying homeostatic behavior.
source: Finally, we propose that investigating large-scale network dynamics can reveal an additional layer of insight into the principles underlying homeostatic behavior, which might be overlooked when studies are restricted to the observation and perturbation of smaller subpopulations.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion about the value of network-level analysis.
